Of course the problems with his ideas run deeper than this; they stem from some fundamental misapprehensions about our situation. This is not only a tendency with Lama, but a misapprehension on the parts of most other "rugged individualists" and laissez faire libertarians. They're living in a matrix, a dream that exists in their own minds and nowhere else. It causes them to ignore reality and their causal responsibility in it. Not really. We all live in that system and participate within it, even if one likes to imagine that they do not. If you're part of a community buying basic commodities (including stores of energy), paying taxes, and banking within that society, you are part of the system. You didn't chose it. No one alive today chose it. These are forces beyond most people's comprehension; they are global. We aren't talking about this or that political choice, trend, historical phase, it's the evolution of mankind we're dealing with. We are all caught up in it. The true hold-outs are few and far in between, and the majority of people who believe themselves to be these hold-outs are not.

But let's deal with the problem of fear in the economy. Some irrational idea takes hold of a sufficient number of people in one community. Those people get the notion that they are going to face a shortage of toilet paper - we can ignore whether the possibility is realistic or not. What's relevant is the facticity of the impulse. So one wave of consumers clears the shelves of toilet paper at a handful of stores in a community. This causes the next wave of consumers to become alarmed at merely the sight of an empty store shelf (hold in mind this all has to do with a feeling of safety and relative abundance - we depend on it). They go to the neighboring community, and as a result of their alarm begin to do the same there. Soon that community sends waves of its own to gather the resources from their neighboring community's stores until all of that resource is hoarded for a given region.

So what? It's just toilet paper. This is where the overal impression and feeling become important. A person who wanders into the first store after the clearing event is likely to think to themselves (even if unconsciously): "shortage". Not an anxiety without an object, but a creeping kind of fear with one object: not enough > hunger > death. If that person can't have the toilet paper they need, then there is a vague problem in their sphere of experience, and now they'll go fill the hole with beef. "Yes, I'll stock up on meat," they say.

Repeat the entire phenomenon just described, now with beef. It has nothing to do with rationality. It has everything to do with fear and game theory. One cannot know what is coming with certainty, and more importantly, they cannot know what the people around them will do. This vague dissolution of trust results in a patterned behavior to secure one's immortality with tangible goods, tangible reaches. Everyone is now in playing a game of poker.

"So what?", says someone like Llama. "More power to the people who are going to survive." This is where the cracks in understanding begin to show. There is no real food shortage. I live in a community of farmers, I grew up in one, and I have several friends today who farm at a relatively large level. We aren't slowing down our food production. There is no indication that we face a food shortage at all. The provisional shortage is happening because of frightened behavior at the last stage in the supply chain, and our economies are not designed for this sort of pull from that end. They aren't designed to prepare every member of the economy for an arbitrary period of time. They are designed to run relatively lean. We wouldn't have a problem if people were not changing their food buying behaviors, but, there was the problem of the toilet paper, the problem of the empty shelf, that lead to the problem of the empty refrigerator, which leads to the problem of the empty store, which leads to the problem of the empty banks when people go and pull their money from their accounts. We cannot analyze this at only one level of the economy as Llama is doing, we have to think about this at a systems level.

It becomes clear to see how we are all part of this system, and nobody chose it. Again, if you purchase, participate, and bank within a community, you are part of it. You're a cog in that system whose every public action is parcel to the ongoing churn. The people who deny this are dreaming. Your dollar is the same dollar as your neighbor's, after all.

It is in everyone's interest to stop the flow of that fear, and the behaviors that create it, as soon as possible, before a level is reached where the toppling dominoes cannot be stopped, i.e. we cannot run fast enough to catch up to the front of the wave. There's a worse virus that can move through a society than a flu, and it is called fear. Every system within society that you can think of is designed to manage that. You're a part of the system if you are in or adjacent to that system at all.

The only possibility for you to be totally extricated from the global network of human society would be to truly live in the wilderness, far and away from all contact. There may be a handful of people in the mountains, for example, that could go on.

It is in everyone's interest to discourage panicked hoarding. It's far, far more than a case of "Beat ya to it! You should have thought faster!". This isn't first come, first serve at the garage sale. It's about maintaining the adequate flow of energy through society. When that flow is thrown off too greatly, society will collapse. You do not want this. People who think they want this don't understand. Everything changed when humans covered the earth. Things were different in an era when there was still frontier, space to spread out. Humans have spread across the planet like a virus, because on a metaphysical level that is what we are. We've crossed a threshold that there is no going back from.

It gets deeper than this as well, but it's too particular and would take too much time. To bring it all home, let's confirm what makes this situation truly unique. It would be different if we are actually dealing with an event that was going to wipe out a massive part of the population. Take a story like the Walking Dead. What made it possible for the social dynamics of that show to play out across the seasons was the fact that most people died from the threat. This is not true of our case.
